title: Java gives you several ready-made executors: newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newScheduledThreadPool, and ForkJoinPool. When would you pick each one? Why is ForkJoinPool excellent for CPU-heavy recursive work but a poor choice for blocking IO?
shortTitle: Fixed vs Cached vs Scheduled pool?
keyPoints: Fixed thread pool: constant number of threads for steady, bounded workload. Predictable resource usage but unbounded queue risk.
Cached thread pool: creates threads on demand, reuses idle ones. Good for short bursty tasks but unbounded thread creation for slow tasks.
Scheduled thread pool: runs tasks after a delay or on a repeating schedule. scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay.
ForkJoinPool: work-stealing deques for recursive divide-and-conquer. Excellent for CPU-bound recursion, poor for blocking IO.
ForkJoinPool is poor for IO because it is sized to roughly one thread per core, and blocked workers cannot steal or be stolen from.
In production, use ThreadPoolExecutor directly with bounded queues instead of the Executors factory methods.
The common ForkJoinPool is shared across the entire JVM; blocking IO on it stalls all parallel streams and default CompletableFutures.

s1_definition.oneliner: Choose fixed for steady bounded load, cached for short bursts, scheduled for timed/periodic jobs, and ForkJoinPool for CPU-bound recursion, but never use ForkJoinPool for blocking IO because its core-sized pool stalls when workers block.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fixed thread pool** – constant core and max size, unbounded queue. Predictable resource use for steady workloads. Danger: unbounded queue can OOM.
- **Cached thread pool** – zero core, unlimited max, SynchronousQueue. Creates a thread per task if no idle thread is available. Good for short bursty tasks. Danger: slow tasks create unbounded threads.
- **Scheduled thread pool** – runs tasks after a delay or on a repeating schedule. `scheduleAtFixedRate` anchors to a clock; `scheduleWithFixedDelay` adds a gap after each completion.
- **ForkJoinPool** – work-stealing deques, sized to approximately the number of cores. Excellent for recursive divide-and-conquer (parallel array sum, merge sort). Poor for blocking IO because blocked workers cannot steal and cores sit idle.
- **Common pool** – `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` is shared JVM-wide by parallel streams and default CompletableFutures. Blocking IO on it stalls everything.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India: fixed pool = a branch with exactly 10 tellers hired for the year. Cached pool = a branch that hires a temp the instant a customer walks in and lets temps go after a minute idle. Scheduled pool = the clerk who runs the interest posting job every night at 2 AM. ForkJoinPool = a team that splits a huge counting job into halves, halves of halves, and whoever finishes early grabs work from a busy colleague.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Executor Choice Decision Tree
  ═════════════════════════════

  Is the work CPU-bound recursive?
    YES → ForkJoinPool (work-stealing)
    NO
      ↓
  Is the work periodic/timed?
    YES → ScheduledThreadPool
    NO
      ↓
  Is the workload steady and bounded?
    YES → ThreadPoolExecutor (bounded queue)
    NO
      ↓
  Short bursty tasks?
    YES → Cached (with caution) or bounded pool
    NO → ThreadPoolExecutor with IO-bound sizing
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java provides four executor shapes for different workloads. Fixed pools for steady bounded work with predictable resource usage. Cached pools for short bursty tasks that arrive in waves. Scheduled pools for timed and periodic execution. ForkJoinPool for CPU-bound recursive divide-and-conquer.

ForkJoinPool excels at CPU recursion because work-stealing keeps all cores busy. It fails at blocking IO because it is sized to roughly one thread per core, and blocked workers cannot steal or be stolen from. The common pool is shared JVM-wide, so blocking IO on it stalls all parallel streams and default CompletableFutures everywhere in the application.

In production, use ThreadPoolExecutor directly with bounded queues and rejection policies for fixed pools, and never use cached pools for slow or blocking tasks. Keep the ForkJoinPool common pool reserved for CPU-bound work and give blocking IO its own dedicated bounded executor.

At National Bank of India, parallel stream for VaR computation stalled because HTTP calls blocked common pool workers. Moving IO to a dedicated pool of 30 threads freed the common pool for CPU work, reducing VaR latency from 500ms to 50ms.

Remember one sentence: use fixed pools for steady work, scheduled for timed jobs, ForkJoinPool for CPU recursion, and never run blocking IO on the common pool.
